# Māratajjanīya Sutta (MN 50 (PTS MN i 332))

**ID:** MN 50 (PTS MN i 332)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Māratajjanīya Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Rebuke of Māra
**PTS:** MN i 332

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Māratajjanīya Sutta* (MN 50) is a narrative-driven discourse in the Majjhimanikāya in which narrative elements far outweigh doctrinal exposition [Sujato & Brahmali 2015]. The sutta begins with Māra entering the belly of Mahāmoggallāna; recognizing him, the elder confronts the tempter and delivers a stern sermon warning of the perils of harassing the disciples of an enlightened teacher [SuttaCentral; Bingenheimer; Dayal 1932]. In this discourse—the only canonical occasion where Moggallāna recounts his own past existences—he reveals that in a distant past under the Buddha Kakusandha he had himself been a Māra named Dūsī, for whose unwholesome deeds against noble disciples he suffered severe retributive rebirth [Dayal 1932; Appleton 2010; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Within this recollection, Moggallāna also recounts how Kakusandha's foremost disciple Sañjīva once entered the attainment of cessation beneath a tree and was mistaken for dead by locals, who built and ignited a funeral pyre around him from which he emerged completely unscathed [Polak 2011]. The discourse also mentions alternate designations for the great hell (*Mahāniraya*), including *Chaphassāyatanika* and *Saṅkusamāhata* [Marino 2017]. Scholars note that such narrative recollections in the early discourses function as early prototypes of the *apadāna* life-story genre [Sujato 2012].

MN 50 shares extensive textual reuse with the *Mahāmoggallānattheragāthā* (Thag 20.1, vv. 1187–1208), which presents identical closing verses spoken by Moggallāna following his encounter with Māra [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Multiple cross-language parallels exist: three Chinese versions are preserved, including a sutra in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 131, T 26) and two independent translations, the *Mo raoluan jing* (T 66) and the *Bimo shi mulian jing* (T 67, ca. 250 CE) [Bingenheimer; SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Parallel Sanskrit fragments are cataloged as SF 279 and SHT sutta 42 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. A comparative detail noted between versions is that while the *Madhyama-āgama* parallel depicts laypeople spreading their hair on the ground out of respect instigated by Māra, MN 50 lacks this specific motif [Anālayo].
